Non-1:1 Relationships in the SomaScan Menu

Source: vignettes/mapping-analytes-to-genes.Rmd
mapping-analytes-to-genes.Rmd

This R package is an in-development resource and is research use only.

Overview

The SomaScan menu contains instances of non-1:1 relationships between SOMAmer® Reagents and their target proteins. In simple terms, this means there is sometimes not a perfect, singular line that can be drawn between one SOMAmer Reagent, its target protein, and the gene that transcribes it. This is a unique characteristic of SomaScan, stemming from the biological complexity and diversity of the proteome. Understanding and handling these non-1:1 relationships can be a crucial processing step for pathway analysis, particularly when using tools or methods developed for gene-based (transcriptomic) data.

This vignette will explain why these relationships are relevant to pathway analysis, and demonstrate how the tools in SomaEnrich can be used to streamline a pathway analysis workflow.

How SomaScan Measures Proteins

To better understand non-1:1 relationships in the SomaScan menu, and how their presence shapes data analysis, it first helps to know how the assay works.

SOMAmer Reagents bind to three-dimensional protein structures, like epitopes, and are conceptually similar to monoclonal antibodies in immunoassays. Because SomaScan measures specific structural features, rather than entire proteins, a single protein can be detected by multiple SOMAmer Reagents if it contains multiple distinct binding structures.

So, for example, the following 1:many pattern could be observed in the data:

Protein 1 ____ SOMAmer Reagent 1
        |_____ SOMAmer Reagent 2
        |_____ SOMAmer Reagent 3

This differs from non-affinity-based protein measurement technologies like mass spectrometry, where measurements typically correspond more directly to individual proteins or genes.

With this context in mind, the remainder of this vignette will use example SomaScan data and R code to show what non-1:1 relationships look like in the data, how they impact gene-based analyses like GSEA, and options for handling them.

Load R Packages 

library(SomaDataIO)
library(SomaEnrich)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

Prepare for GSEA

In pre-ranked GSEA, an ordered statistical metric is required, often derived from the results of differential expression analysis. This can be pulled from the SomaEnrich::t_tests data set. The t_stat will be used as the ranking metric - please note that this may not be the best metric for your experiment, and is merely used here as an example.

Entrez gene symbols will be used as vector names, to match the gene set networks already available in SomaEnrich. Below is a subset of the t_tests data set, sorted by |t_stat|:

t_tests |>
    select(SeqId, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat) |>
    arrange(desc(abs(t_stat))) |>
    head(n = 10)
## # A tibble: 10 × 3
##    SeqId    EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat
##    <chr>    <chr>             <dbl>
##  1 8468-19  KLK3             -14.5 
##  2 6580-29  PZP               14.3 
##  3 21232-39 KLK3             -13.4 
##  4 7926-13  SPINT3           -13.3 
##  5 13699-6  KLK3             -10.8 
##  6 4330-4   KLK3              -9.94
##  7 3032-11  CGA|FSHB           9.53
##  8 16892-23 ENPP2              8.86
##  9 2953-31  CGA|LHB            8.71
## 10 5763-67  DEFB104A          -8.14

Every SeqId in the above table is unique. However, some genes, like Prostate-Specific Antigen (KLK3), appear multiple times in the “EntrezGeneSymbol” column. This illustrates a 1:many (i.e. non-1:1) relationship between KLK3 and SeqIds in the data.

If Entrez gene symbols are solely used to identify each data point in the ranked vector, an input vector for GSEA could look like this:

rank_vec <- t_tests$t_stat
names(rank_vec) <- t_tests$EntrezGeneSymbol

rank_vec[1:10]
##       KLK3        PZP       KLK3     SPINT3       KLK3       KLK3 
## -14.541600  14.285305 -13.369361 -13.307083 -10.835849  -9.940982 
##   CGA|FSHB      ENPP2    CGA|LHB   DEFB104A 
##   9.528913   8.862328   8.709291  -8.141046

In the top example entries alone, some gene names are seen more than once, and combined gene entities with a “|” character are present in the vector names. Both of these patterns are unique to SomaScan-derived data and can complicate the GSEA workflow.

In particular, the presence of duplicate entries may have unintended consequences for GSEA, if not corrected, as it violates one of the core assumptions of GSEA.

Assumptions of GSEA

A critical assumption of the GSEA algorithm is that 1:1 mapping is present between ranked entries and biological entities, and that each gene in the ranked list is only represented once (A. Subramanian 2005; “GSEA Software Documentation” 2026). Violations of this assumption can disproportionately weight genes during calculation of the enrichment score, resulting in the following undesirable effects:

  • Hits (highly-ranked genes found in a gene set) could be counted multiple times
  • Incidences of multiple counting could create inflated enrichment scores
  • Enrichment scores for small gene sets could be especially distorted

The non-1:1 gene:SOMAmer Reagent relationships in the SomaScan menu stress this assumption when using SomaScan-derived ranking statistics for GSEA.

SOMAmer Reagent Targets

In a SomaScan data set, SOMAmer Reagents and SeqIds have a 1:1 relationship, where each SeqId uniquely identifies a single SOMAmer reagent. However, as described earlier in this document, proteins do not necessarily have a 1:1 relationship with a single SOMAmer Reagent. In these cases, external identifiers like the UniProt ID (or gene ID) may not fully distinguish the exact target structure of a SOMAmer Reagent.

For example, as observed earlier, the KLK3 gene appears in the 11K SomaScan menu multiple times:

## # A tibble: 4 × 5
##   SeqId    TargetFullName               Target UniProt EntrezGeneSymbol
##   <chr>    <chr>                        <chr>  <chr>   <chr>           
## 1 13699-6  Prostate-specific antigen    PSA    P07288  KLK3            
## 2 21232-39 Benign Prostate specific An… BPSA   P07288  KLK3            
## 3 4330-4   Prostate-specific antigen    PSA    P07288  KLK3            
## 4 8468-19  Prostate-specific antigen    PSA    P07288  KLK3

All 3 SeqIds in the above table are unique, but the other values are (for the most part) identical. In the example_data_11k ADAT, all these unique analytes are present, each with a distinct RFU measurement:

## # A tibble: 10 × 5
##    SampleId seq.13699.6 seq.21232.39 seq.4330.4 seq.8468.19
##    <chr>          <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>
##  1 23              898.        3642.       377.       2088.
##  2 119             182.         320        141.        368.
##  3 66              714.        2301.       282        1289 
##  4 46              185.         514.       132.        324.
##  5 200169          542.        2055.       277.        898.
##  6 51              334.         505        182.        424.
##  7 174             171.         376.       158.        912.
##  8 177             314.         397.       164.        379.
##  9 147             642.        2355.       315.       1655.
## 10 86              204.         329.       120.        373.

In t_tests, multiple analytes targeting KLK3 were (after sorting) located near the bottom of the ranked gene vector.

So, let’s return to the example vector we made for pre-ranked GSEA. Proceeding with this vector as-is may have the following unintended effects:

  • KLK3 appears multiple times in the ranked vector, potentially leading to over-representation of KLK3 in the final GSEA results
    • This effect applies to any other duplicated entities in the vector
  • The vector elements with “|”-delimited names will not match gene symbols in the available GO or MSigDB resources, and consequently will be counted as a “miss” in the enrichment score calculation, rather than a hit
    • This can result in inaccurate counting of these highly-ranked entities in the final enrichment results

Solutions for both of these points are implemented by SomaEnrich, and will be described in greater detail below.

Solutions in SomaEnrich

The functions in SomaEnrich automatically handle instances of 1:many mapping between SOMAmer Reagents (and therefore, SomaScan measurements) and external gene or protein identifiers.

SomaEnrich provides functions that perform:

  1. Data cleaning operations, to split apart delimited identifiers that signify protein heterodimers
  2. Measurement filtering and selection, to resolve non-1:1 mapping for gene-based analyses like GSEA

The following sections will explain how functions in SomaEnrich handle these scenarios.

Working with Heterodimers and “|” Delimiters

The SomaScan menu contains instances where a “|” character is used to delineate two (or more) gene or protein identifiers. This notation indicates that a given SOMAmer Reagent binds a heterodimer protein or larger protein heterocomplex, where the protein subunits originate from different genes. To fully capture this information in the menu, all genes with protein products in the complex are separated by a delimiter character, typically “|”.

However, the biological knowledge bases typically used by popular pathway analysis tools, like GO and KEGG, were developed for gene-centric data, and do not contain this type of annotation.

When performing GSEA, all identifiers used for analysis inputs should be of consistent type, and in the same format. By default, SomaEnrich uses Entrez gene symbols for both GO and MSigDB gene sets; therefore, the gene symbols in the ranked input vector must be compatible Entrez gene symbols. Because this heterodimer gene notation is unique to SomaScan, genes delimited by “|” will not be compatible with the entries in GO and MSigDB. Consequently, any gene in the input vector not found in the gene set will contribute to the negative increment of the running sum statistic, but will not be removed from the data set (A. Subramanian 2005). This can affect the calculation of the enrichment score - if a highly-ranked gene should contribute to the running sum, but can’t be correctly matched to any member of the gene set, the enrichment contribution from that gene will not be adequately captured.

To ensure consistency in gene symbols across both input ranks and gene sets, delimited identifiers are split prior to analysis (see the split_ids argument of SomaEnrich::somaPrGSEA()).

Here’s a preview of the first 10 rows of data, without the splitting operation:

# Prior to split
t_tests |>
    select(AptName, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat) |>
    head(n = 10)
## # A tibble: 10 × 3
##    AptName      EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat
##    <chr>        <chr>             <dbl>
##  1 seq.8468.19  KLK3             -14.5 
##  2 seq.6580.29  PZP               14.3 
##  3 seq.21232.39 KLK3             -13.4 
##  4 seq.7926.13  SPINT3           -13.3 
##  5 seq.13699.6  KLK3             -10.8 
##  6 seq.4330.4   KLK3              -9.94
##  7 seq.3032.11  CGA|FSHB           9.53
##  8 seq.16892.23 ENPP2              8.86
##  9 seq.2953.31  CGA|LHB            8.71
## 10 seq.5763.67  DEFB104A          -8.14

And here is that same data post-split:

t_tests_split <- t_tests |>
    select(AptName, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat) |>
    mutate(row_id = row_number()) |>
    tidyr::separate_rows(EntrezGeneSymbol, sep = "\\|")

head(t_tests_split, n = 12)
## # A tibble: 12 × 4
##    AptName      EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat row_id
##    <chr>        <chr>             <dbl>  <int>
##  1 seq.8468.19  KLK3             -14.5       1
##  2 seq.6580.29  PZP               14.3       2
##  3 seq.21232.39 KLK3             -13.4       3
##  4 seq.7926.13  SPINT3           -13.3       4
##  5 seq.13699.6  KLK3             -10.8       5
##  6 seq.4330.4   KLK3              -9.94      6
##  7 seq.3032.11  CGA                9.53      7
##  8 seq.3032.11  FSHB               9.53      7
##  9 seq.16892.23 ENPP2              8.86      8
## 10 seq.2953.31  CGA                8.71      9
## 11 seq.2953.31  LHB                8.71      9
## 12 seq.5763.67  DEFB104A          -8.14     10

This splitting procedure can have the following effects:

  1. Splitting the heterodimers requires duplicating the ranking metric value, which can introduce ties to the ranked vector
  2. Splitting the heterodimers can contribute to instances of gene name duplication in the ranked input vector

Let’s use the table above to better illustrate the first point. The following analyte, seq.4914.10, maps to 3 Entrez gene symbols:

t_tests |>
    dplyr::select(AptName, SeqId, Target, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat) |>
    filter(AptName == "seq.4914.10")
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##   AptName     SeqId   Target EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat
##   <chr>       <chr>   <chr>  <chr>             <dbl>
## 1 seq.4914.10 4914-10 HCG    CGA|CGB3|CGB7      7.90

The string CGA|CGB3|CGB7 is unlikely to be matched in any gene-based database, so the string must be split into its constituent parts:

t_tests |>
    dplyr::select(AptName, SeqId, Target, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat) |>
    filter(AptName == "seq.4914.10") |>
    tidyr::separate_rows(EntrezGeneSymbol, sep = "\\|")
## # A tibble: 3 × 5
##   AptName     SeqId   Target EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat
##   <chr>       <chr>   <chr>  <chr>             <dbl>
## 1 seq.4914.10 4914-10 HCG    CGA                7.90
## 2 seq.4914.10 4914-10 HCG    CGB3               7.90
## 3 seq.4914.10 4914-10 HCG    CGB7               7.90

Now, if we were to use the t_stat as input into somaPrGSEA(), the input would look like this:

##      CGA     CGB3     CGB7 
## 7.895289 7.895289 7.895289

The genes are unique, but the actual values used for ranking the genes are the same. This can produce a warning during GSEA, stating that the ranking vector has ties. Essentially, these 3 elements can’t be ranked properly, because they all have the same ranking value. While this is typically undesirable if it occurs in the raw, unmodified ranking vector, the decision to split heterodimers during pre-processing can itself create ties. This is expected behavior when splitting SomaScan heterodimers.

Multiple Targets Map to One Gene

Let’s move on to the second unintended effect of splitting heterodimers: it can contribute to instances of gene name duplication in the ranked input vector. This may result in >1 value per AptName, with a unique gene symbol for each value. Take 3032-11, for example; prior to the split operation, it possesses one t_stat value:

filter(t_tests, AptName == "seq.3032.11") |>
    select(AptName, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat)
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   AptName     EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat
##   <chr>       <chr>             <dbl>
## 1 seq.3032.11 CGA|FSHB           9.53

Post-split, the t_stat value for 3032-11 is split across multiple rows.

filter(t_tests_split, AptName == "seq.3032.11")
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   AptName     EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat row_id
##   <chr>       <chr>             <dbl>  <int>
## 1 seq.3032.11 CGA                9.53      7
## 2 seq.3032.11 FSHB               9.53      7

Because genes like CGA can be mapped to >1 SOMAmer Reagent, the above step produces multiple t_stat values for CGA, when viewed in combination with the rest of the data set:

filter(t_tests_split, EntrezGeneSymbol == "CGA")
## # A tibble: 5 × 4
##   AptName     EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat row_id
##   <chr>       <chr>             <dbl>  <int>
## 1 seq.3032.11 CGA               9.53       7
## 2 seq.2953.31 CGA               8.71       9
## 3 seq.4914.10 CGA               7.90      12
## 4 seq.14056.4 CGA               3.34     128
## 5 seq.3521.16 CGA              -0.409   4853

All of these values are associated with the gene CGA, but it’s best practice to not use this vector as-is for GSEA. To avoid duplication of gene identifiers, only one t_stat value for CGA will be chosen. But why only choose one, and how should it be selected?

Selecting One Measurement per Gene

In transcriptomics, it’s common practice to combine transcript or probe-based measurements and sum them to obtain gene-level counts. When performing GSEA with SomaScan data, it may be tempting to apply this methodology and, for example, sum together all measurements from analytes mapping to CGA or KLK3. This would produce one single measurement for each gene and resolve the identifier duplication problem described previously.

However, it is not advised to collapse or aggregate analytes into a single entity based on their protein target or gene. Instead, it is standard practice to keep SomaScan measurements distinct whenever possible.

If each SOMAmer Reagent is measuring a different isoform or region of a protein, collapsing these data points may lose valuable information about those protein regions. Instead, it is recommended to treat each analyte as an independent measurement, and select a single “best” measurement to be representative of each protein (or, in this case, gene) when multiple measurements are present.

But what constitutes the “best” measurement? This can can vary depending on experiment and ranking metric used for pre-ranked GSEA. SomaEnrich provides a few different methods to make this selection.

Let’s return to the KLK3 example; we will sort the KLK3 analytes by our chosen ranking metric (t_stat):

filter(t_tests, EntrezGeneSymbol == ex_gene) |>
    select(AptName, EntrezGeneSymbol, t_stat) |>
    arrange(desc(t_stat))
## # A tibble: 4 × 3
##   AptName      EntrezGeneSymbol t_stat
##   <chr>        <chr>             <dbl>
## 1 seq.4330.4   KLK3              -9.94
## 2 seq.13699.6  KLK3             -10.8 
## 3 seq.21232.39 KLK3             -13.4 
## 4 seq.8468.19  KLK3             -14.5

The “top” KLK3-associated analyte (sorted by t_stat) is seq.4330.4. If we follow the recommendation to retain one measurement per gene and arbitrarily choose the first occurrence, only this t_stat value for KLK3 will be used for input into GSEA, and the others will be lost. However, this can have unintended consequences. What if we’re interested in the value with the largest magnitude, regardless of sign? Or what if the selected ranking metric is a p-value? The same sorting method may not work for both p-values (where the smallest value is preferred) and fold change values (where the largest absolute value is preferred).

Merely sorting in ascending/descending order and choosing the first occurrence may not return the expected result.

Selection Methods in SomaEnrich

SomaEnrich performs this sorting and selection step under the hood in somaPrGSEA() via the resolve_multimapping argument. When resolve_multimapping = TRUE (the default), the function will create a catalog of all unique genes present in a ranked data frame, identify all SOMAmer Reagents associated with each gene, and select a single analyte based on a user-defined criteria. By default, the statistic with the largest absolute value is retained. This ensures that each protein target/gene is only represented once in the data set, without collapsing values to create a single summed measurement.

However, like mentioned previously, this sorting method may not be appropriate for all ranking metrics. The following measurement sorting and filtering methods are supported:

  • Filtering by absolute value (the default): the largest absolute value is chosen (ignores sign)
  • Filtering by maximum: the maximum value is chosen
  • Filtering by minimum: the minimum value is chosen
  • Filtering by rank: the smallest rank is chosen using pre-sorted data

For more complex sorting (i.e. using two or more sorting criteria), the “rank” method may be more appropriate. After sorting by the desired criteria, like a combination of FC and p-value in a single-sided test, a rank is assigned to the input values, using the order in which they were sorted in. The first value is ranked 1. In cases of multimapping, the value with the lowest rank is retained.

Please note that selection by “rank” and “minimum” can produce different results! Filtering by rank selects based on position in the input vector (given pre-sorting), while filtering by minimum selects based on actual numeric value, and can be impacted by the presence of negative values when the metric is signed. Similarly, depending on how the pre-sorting is done, “maximum” and “rank” can select either the same or different values. Ultimately, filtering by rank may lose information - the magnitude of difference in values is ignored, and proximity to the start of the vector is prioritized. Alternatively, if selecting by absolute value, magnitude of signal is prioritized, while directionality (i.e. sign) is lost.

The chunk below shows how the available sorting options can identify different values for fictional GENE_A:

gene_a <- c(GENE_A = 0.01, GENE_A = -0.5, GENE_A = 5, GENE_A = -10)

max(gene_a)
## [1] 5
min(gene_a)
## [1] -10
max(abs(gene_a))
## [1] 10
sort(gene_a, decreasing = TRUE)[[1]] # "rank" option selects the 1st value when sorted
## [1] 5

The code above highlights the importance of assessing which selection method is most appropriate for your data. Multiplied over hundreds of cases of non-1:1 mapping, the chosen measurement filtering method can have a notable impact on GSEA data.

After applying the filtering technique described above to the example rank vector, the results should look like this:

##       KLK3        PZP     SPINT3        CGA       FSHB      ENPP2 
## -14.541600  14.285305 -13.307083   9.528913   9.528913   8.862328 
##        LHB   DEFB104A     CRISP2       CGB3 
##   8.709291  -8.141046  -8.096695   7.895289

No duplicate genes or “|”-delimited heterodimers remain in the preview of the ranking vector.

This filtering procedure is performed for all genes in the input ranked vector, and the filtered vector will then be used as input for GSEA.

The output of somaPrGSEA() will include this filtered and modified vector, for reference.

Summary

  • The SomaScan menu contains non-1:1 relationships between SOMAmer Reagents and their target proteins/genes, which can complicate gene-centric analyses like GSEA
  • Delimited identifiers (e.g., “GENE1|GENE2”) must be split so each symbol can be properly matched to gene sets
  • SomaLogic recommends keeping analyte measurements distinct rather than collapsing or aggregating them by gene — this preserves valuable information about protein isoforms and regions
  • SomaEnrich automatically handles non-1:1 relationships by selecting a single “best” measurement per gene, rather than summing measurements together
  • “Best” measurement can be defined in various ways, and a few options are provided to do this automatically
  • The R functions prepareRanks(), somaPrGSEA(), and somaORA() are capable of performing these processing steps

Please keep in mind that these processing steps are an optional feature, and ultimately you must decide if they are appropriate for your analysis.
